<reason>Both sides were sharp and the debate narrowed cleanly to one question: what the motion adds beyond existing platform defaults, and whether that addition is proportionate. PRO landed real hits — CON's opening concession that minors don't fund free access gutted the motion's "even if" clause, and the "dollar-blind" point (a PIN approves a currency pack, not the forty hidden-odds pulls that follow) was PRO's best move. But CON adapted better across rounds: it reframed the concession as raising PRO's harm bar, answered both pressure questions directly and in format, introduced a genuine distinguishing feature (casinos pay withdrawable cash; loot boxes don't) that PRO never answered in its closing, and then turned PRO's own delivery-capacity line against it — a fixed $20 bankroll loaded by a parent and then emptying is exactly the "claw machine with a coin pocket" PRO had carved out. CON's closing exposed that what remains of the motion is mechanic regulation of a deliberate parent's authorized budget, and PRO's final speech didn't squarely rebut that reframing. CON's claim that authentication is default-on everywhere is somewhat overconfident and sits awkwardly with its earlier "one toggle away" framing, and PRO's odds-disclosure point was more labeled than answered, which keeps this competitive. PRO also absorbed more execution cost with three clipped turns. Narrow but real CON win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's B5.1–B5.2 closing turn: taking PRO's "twenty dollars becomes forty pulls behind the bedroom door" image and showing the child cannot pull a forty-first time without another parental act, then recasting it as the claw-machine-with-an-emptying-pocket case PRO itself had exempted — converting PRO's central metaphor and its own line-drawing into evidence that the motion regulates mechanics, not spending.</best_rebuttal>
